knowledgeBase.summary: Practical cybersecurity reference covering core security principles, the current threat landscape, authentication/MFA, encryption, network and endpoint security, incident response, and hardening checklists — built for daily IT/security decision-making rather than certification trivia.

sections.title: Security Fundamentals
sections.content:
The CIA triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) is the foundation every security control maps back to: confidentiality prevents unauthorized disclosure, integrity prevents unauthorized modification, availability keeps systems usable for legitimate users. A control that improves one can weaken another (e.g. aggressive lockout policies improve confidentiality but hurt availability), so trade-offs must be explicit.

Core principles applied daily:
Least privilege — every account, service, and process gets only the access it needs, nothing more. Audit permissions periodically; access accumulates over time ("privilege creep") as roles change.
Defense in depth — no single control is trusted alone. A compromised firewall shouldn't mean a compromised database; layer network, host, application, and data controls.
Zero trust — never trust based on network location alone ("inside the LAN" is not a security boundary). Every request is authenticated and authorized regardless of origin.
Fail secure — when a control fails, it should fail to the safe state (e.g. a failed auth check denies access, a failed firewall rule blocks rather than allows).

Risk is commonly expressed as Risk = Likelihood x Impact. Practical triage: rank findings by exploitability and business impact, not just CVSS score alone — an internal, low-CVSS misconfiguration exposing customer data can matter more than a high-CVSS bug on an isolated dev box.

Security is a process, not a product: patching, monitoring, and reviewing access are ongoing operational duties, not one-time deployments.

sections.title: Threat Landscape
sections.content:
Phishing remains the most common initial-access vector. Variants: spear phishing (targeted, researched), whaling (targets executives), smishing/vishing (SMS/voice), and business email compromise (BEC — impersonating a vendor or executive to redirect payments). Defense is layered: email filtering, DMARC/SPF/DKIM, user training, and MFA so a stolen password alone isn't enough.

Ransomware typically arrives via phishing, exposed RDP, or a vulnerable public-facing service, then moves laterally (often via SMB admin shares or stolen domain admin credentials) before encrypting and exfiltrating data for double-extortion. Segmented networks and offline/immutable backups are the main mitigations — backups reachable from the same compromised domain are not real backups.

Supply chain attacks compromise a trusted upstream component (a library, an update mechanism, an MSP) to reach many downstream victims at once — verify package integrity (checksums, lockfiles) and limit third-party access scope.

Insider threats (malicious or negligent) are mitigated by least privilege, access logging, and separation of duties rather than pure perimeter defense.

Social engineering exploits human trust rather than technical flaws — pretexting, tailgating into secure areas, or a fake IT support call requesting a password reset. No technical control fully substitutes for trained, skeptical staff.

Other common patterns: credential stuffing (reused passwords tried against many services), exploitation of unpatched CVEs within days of public disclosure, and misconfigured cloud storage (public S3 buckets, open blob containers) as a leading cause of large data exposures.

sections.title: Authentication & MFA
sections.content:
Authentication factors: something you know (password), something you have (token, phone), something you are (biometric). MFA requires two or more distinct factor categories — a password plus a security question is NOT MFA (both are "something you know").

MFA methods, weakest to strongest: SMS OTP (vulnerable to SIM-swap), authenticator app TOTP (RFC 6238, e.g. Google/Microsoft Authenticator), push notification (convenient but vulnerable to "MFA fatigue" — attacker spams approval requests until the user taps accept), and FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keys (phishing-resistant — the cryptographic challenge is bound to the origin domain, so a fake login page can't relay it).

Single Sign-On (SSO) via SAML or OIDC centralizes authentication — one strong credential (ideally with FIDO2 MFA) instead of many weak ones, and centralizes revocation when an employee leaves.

Password policy guidance has shifted (NIST SP 800-63B): prioritize length over forced complexity/rotation, check new passwords against known-breached password lists, and don't force periodic changes for passwords not known to be compromised — forced rotation historically pushed users toward predictable patterns (Password1!, Password2!).

Directory/auth protocols an IT professional will hit: LDAP (directory queries), Kerberos (ticket-based auth in AD environments — watch for "Golden Ticket"/"Kerberoasting" attacks against service accounts with weak passwords), and RADIUS (network device / VPN authentication).

Credential stuffing defense: rate limiting, CAPTCHA on repeated failures, and mandatory MFA — since the credentials being tried are often valid (reused from another breach), password strength alone doesn't help.

sections.title: Encryption Basics
sections.content:
Symmetric encryption (AES-256 is the current standard) uses one shared key for both encryption and decryption — fast, used for bulk data, but the key must be distributed securely. Asymmetric encryption (RSA, ECC) uses a public/private key pair — slower, used for key exchange and digital signatures, not bulk data encryption.

TLS combines both: asymmetric crypto negotiates a shared session key during the handshake, then symmetric crypto encrypts the actual traffic. TLS 1.2 is still common; TLS 1.3 is preferred (faster handshake, removed weak cipher support). Always verify with:
openssl s_client -connect host:443 -tls1_3          # test TLS 1.3 support
openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -dates -subject     # check cert validity/expiry
curl -vI https://example.com 2>&1 | grep -i 'ssl\|tls'

Hashing (SHA-256, SHA-3) is one-way — used for integrity checks and password storage, never for "encrypting" something you need back. Passwords must never be stored as raw hashes — use a slow, salted algorithm designed for it: bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 (Argon2id is the current recommendation), which resist GPU-accelerated brute force.
sha256sum file.iso                    # verify file integrity against a published hash
echo -n "text" | openssl dgst -sha256   # quick hash of a string

PKI (Public Key Infrastructure): a Certificate Authority (CA) signs certificates binding a public key to an identity (domain, org). Chain of trust: root CA -> intermediate CA -> leaf certificate. A browser trusts a leaf cert because it trusts the root, and the intermediate links them.

Encryption at rest (disk/database encryption, e.g. LUKS, BitLocker, cloud KMS-managed keys) protects data if storage media is stolen; encryption in transit (TLS, IPsec) protects data crossing a network. Both are needed — neither substitutes for the other.

sections.title: Network Security
sections.content:
Network segmentation limits blast radius: separate VLANs for user workstations, servers, VoIP/telephony, guest Wi-Fi, and management/OOB access, with a firewall or ACL controlling traffic between segments. A compromised guest Wi-Fi device should never be able to reach the internal domain controller.

A DMZ (demilitarized zone) hosts internet-facing services (web servers, mail relays, reverse proxies) in a segment isolated from the internal LAN — if the public-facing box is compromised, the attacker still has to cross another boundary to reach internal systems.

Network Access Control (NAC) — 802.1X — authenticates a device before it gets network access at the switch port level, commonly using RADIUS against a directory service. Without it, plugging any device into an open switch port grants LAN access.

Port security on switches restricts which MAC addresses may connect to a given port and can shut the port down on violation — a basic mitigation against rogue devices and MAC spoofing.

Monitoring: NetFlow/sFlow for traffic patterns, an IDS/IPS (Snort/Suricata) for signature and anomaly-based detection, and centralized logging (syslog to a SIEM) so an incident can be reconstructed after the fact — a network with no logs is a network you can't investigate.

Common quick checks:
nmap -sV -p- target                   # full port scan with service detection (authorized targets only)
ss -tulpn                              # what's listening locally
tcpdump -i eth0 port 443 -w capture.pcap   # capture traffic for later analysis in Wireshark

sections.title: Endpoint Security
sections.content:
Traditional antivirus (signature-based) catches known malware but misses novel/fileless attacks. EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response — CrowdStrike, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, SentinelOne) adds behavioral monitoring, process-tree visibility, and remote response (isolate host, kill process, roll back changes) — the modern baseline for endpoint defense.

Patch management is the single highest-leverage endpoint control: most breaches exploit vulnerabilities that had a patch available for weeks or months. Prioritize by exploitability (is it in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog?) over CVSS score alone, and track patch compliance, not just patch availability.

Application whitelisting/allowlisting (Windows AppLocker, macOS Gatekeeper policies) blocks unapproved executables from running at all — far stronger than blacklisting known-bad files, since it doesn't depend on already knowing about a threat.

Device control: disable or restrict USB mass storage on sensitive endpoints (a classic data-exfiltration and malware-introduction vector); BitLocker/FileVault full-disk encryption protects data if a laptop is lost or stolen.

Hardening basics for any endpoint: disable unused local services, remove local admin rights from standard users (the biggest single reduction in malware's ability to persist/spread), enable host-based firewall, and ensure the endpoint reports into central logging/EDR so an incident on it is visible, not silent.

Mobile Device Management (MDM/Intune, Jamf) extends the same principles — enforced encryption, remote wipe, compliance policies — to phones and tablets accessing corporate resources.

sections.title: Incident Response
sections.content:
Standard IR lifecycle (NIST SP 800-61): Preparation (playbooks, contact lists, tooling in place before an incident), Detection & Analysis (confirm it's real, scope it), Containment (short-term: isolate affected hosts; long-term: patch/rotate credentials while investigation continues), Eradication (remove the actual malware/backdoor/access), Recovery (restore from clean backups, monitor closely), and Lessons Learned (post-incident review — what let it happen, what would have caught it sooner).

First response priorities on a suspected-compromised host: don't power it off (destroys volatile memory evidence) unless actively destructive (e.g. ransomware still encrypting) — isolate it from the network instead (pull the cable / disable the switch port / isolate via EDR) while preserving state.
Triage commands (Linux):
last -20                          # recent logins
w                                  # who's logged in now
ps auxf                            # process tree, look for unexpected parents
netstat -tulpn / ss -tulpn         # unexpected listening ports
find / -mtime -1 -type f 2>/dev/null   # files modified in the last 24h

Chain of custody matters even in internal investigations — document who accessed what evidence and when, in case findings ever need to support HR action, legal proceedings, or law enforcement referral.

Communication discipline: use an out-of-band channel (not the potentially-compromised email/chat system) to coordinate the response, and follow a pre-agreed disclosure process — notifying affected parties/regulators has legal timelines in many jurisdictions (e.g. GDPR's 72-hour breach notification window).

Always run a post-incident review even for near-misses — the goal is a system/process fix, not blame.

sections.title: Security Hardening Checklists
sections.content:
CIS Benchmarks (Center for Internet Security) are the industry-standard hardening baselines for OSes, cloud platforms, and common applications — free to download, mapped to specific config settings with automated scoring tools (CIS-CAT).

Quick Linux server checklist: disable root SSH login (PermitRootLogin no), key-based auth only (PasswordAuthentication no), unattended-upgrades for security patches, ufw/firewalld enabled with a default-deny policy, fail2ban against brute force, remove unused packages/services, and centralized log shipping so this box isn't a blind spot.

Quick Windows server checklist: disable SMBv1, enforce LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) for unique local admin passwords per machine, enable Windows Defender/EDR, restrict RDP to VPN-only or a jump host with MFA, and apply the Microsoft Security Baseline via Group Policy.

Network device checklist: change default credentials immediately, disable unused services (Telnet, HTTP management — use SSH/HTTPS only), restrict management access to a dedicated management VLAN, and keep firmware patched — network gear is frequently the most neglected patch surface in an environment.

Cloud hardening basics: no public storage buckets by default, MFA enforced on all cloud console accounts (especially root/owner accounts), least-privilege IAM roles instead of broad admin grants, and cloud-native logging (CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log) enabled and shipped to a retained location outside the account being audited.

A hardening checklist is a floor, not a ceiling — treat it as the minimum baseline before any environment-specific controls.

sections.title: Phishing Detection and Incident Response
sections.content:
### Phishing Detection and Incident Response

In a B2B telecom/networking environment, phishing often serves as the initial access vector for lateral movement. Detection and response must focus on rapid artifact extraction and automated containment.

#### Detection: Artifact Analysis
When a suspicious email is reported, prioritize header and attachment analysis over body content.

*   **Header Inspection:** Extract `Return-Path`, `Received` chains, and `X-Originating-IP`. Use `dig` or `nslookup` to verify SPF/DKIM/DMARC alignment.
    ```bash
    # Verify SPF record for the sender domain
    dig TXT <sender-domain> +short | grep "v=spf1"
    ```
*   **URL Analysis:** Never click links. Use `curl` to inspect redirects or `whois` to check domain age.
    ```bash
    # Inspect HTTP headers without downloading content
    curl -I -L --max-time 10 <suspicious-url>
    ```
*   **Attachment Sandboxing:** If the environment lacks an automated EDR/Sandbox, use `oleid` or `olevba` (from the `oletools` suite) to inspect Office documents for malicious macros.
    ```bash
    # Scan for suspicious VBA macros
    olevba <malicious_file.docm>
    ```

#### Incident Response: Containment and Eradication
Once a phishing attempt is confirmed, execute the following operational workflow:

1.  **Global Purge:** If using O365/Exchange, use the Exchange Online PowerShell module to remove the message from all user mailboxes immediately.
    ```powershell
    # Search and delete the message globally
    New-ComplianceSearch -Name "PhishPurge" -ExchangeLocation All -ContentMatchQuery 'Subject:"Urgent Invoice"'
    Start-ComplianceSearch -Identity "PhishPurge"
    New-ComplianceSearchAction -SearchName "PhishPurge" -Purge -PurgeType HardDelete
    ```
2.  **Network Containment:** If the user clicked a link or executed a payload, isolate the host at the network layer.
    *   **EDR Isolation:** Trigger host isolation via your EDR (e.g., CrowdStrike `Invoke-FalconHostIsolation` or SentinelOne API).
    *   **Firewall/Proxy:** Block the malicious C2 domain/IP at the perimeter firewall and DNS sinkhole.
        ```bash
        # Example: Null-route malicious IP on Cisco IOS
        ip route <malicious-ip> 255.255.255.255 Null0
        ```
3.  **Credential Reset:** If the user entered credentials, force a password reset and revoke active O365/SAML sessions.
    ```powershell
    # Revoke all refresh tokens for the compromised user
    Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken -ObjectId <user-guid>
    ```

#### Post-Incident Hardening
*   **MFA Enforcement:** Ensure Conditional Access policies require MFA for all B2B/VPN access.
*   **Mail Flow Rules:** Implement strict attachment filtering (block `.exe`, `.scr`, `.js`, `.vbs`) and enable "Safe Links" or equivalent URL rewriting.
*   **Logging:** Ensure `UnifiedAuditLog` (O365) or equivalent logs are ingested into your SIEM with alerts configured for "Impossible Travel" or "New Mail Forwarding Rule" events.

sections.title: Implementing MFA for Linux SSH Access
sections.content:
Implementing Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) for Linux SSH access is a critical defense-in-depth measure to mitigate risks from credential theft and brute-force attacks. For most standard Linux environments, integrating the Google Authenticator PAM (Pluggable Authentication Module) provides a robust, time-based one-time password (TOTP) solution.

### Prerequisites
*   **OpenSSH 9.8p1 or later:** Ensure your SSH daemon is patched against recent vulnerabilities (e.g., CVE-2024-6387).
*   **Out-of-Band Access:** Always maintain an active console or secondary management session during configuration to prevent accidental lockout.

### Implementation Steps

1.  **Install the PAM Module**
    Install the required package for your distribution:
    *   **Debian/Ubuntu:** `sudo apt install libpam-google-authenticator`
    *   **RHEL/AlmaLinux/Fedora:** `sudo dnf install google-authenticator`

2.  **Configure User MFA**
    Run the setup tool for the target user account:
    ```bash
    google-authenticator
    ```
    Follow the prompts. It is recommended to answer `y` to all security questions, including time-based token generation, secret file updates, and rate-limiting. Secure the generated emergency scratch codes in a password manager.

3.  **Configure PAM for SSH**
    Edit `/etc/pam.d/sshd` to include the MFA module. Add the following line at the top of the file:
    ```text
    auth required pam_google_authenticator.so
    ```

4.  **Update SSH Daemon Configuration**
    Modify `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` to enable challenge-response authentication:
    ```text
    ChallengeResponseAuthentication yes
    UsePAM yes
    ```
    To enforce specific authentication flows (e.g., requiring both a public key and an OTP), use the `AuthenticationMethods` directive:
    ```text
    AuthenticationMethods publickey,keyboard-interactive
    ```

5.  **Validate and Restart**
    Test the configuration by opening a new terminal session (do not close the current one). Restart the SSH service to apply changes:
    ```bash
    sudo systemctl restart sshd
    ```

### Operational Considerations
*   **Centralized Management:** For environments with many users, consider enterprise-grade solutions like Duo Security or FreeIPA, which offer centralized reporting and management that manual TOTP setups lack.
*   **Fail2Ban:** Always pair MFA with `fail2ban` to automatically block IPs exhibiting suspicious behavior, reducing the noise of automated attacks.
*   **Hardening:** MFA is not a replacement for SSH best practices. Continue to enforce Ed25519 key-based authentication, disable root login, and move SSH to a non-standard port where appropriate.

sections.title: Red Teaming and Phishing Simulation Frameworks
sections.content:
Effective red teaming and phishing simulations require a balance between realistic adversary emulation and operational stability. In B2B telecom environments, where network availability is critical, prioritize non-disruptive, controlled testing.

### Phishing Simulation: Gophish
Gophish remains the industry standard for open-source phishing simulations due to its simplicity and API-driven architecture.

*   **Configuration:** The `config.json` file controls core server behavior. Ensure strict file permissions (`chmod 640 config.json`) as it contains database credentials.
    *   `admin_server.listen_url`: Set to `127.0.0.1:3333` for local management.
    *   `phish_server.listen_url`: Set to `0.0.0.0:80` (or 443 with valid TLS) for campaign traffic.
*   **Operational Security (OpSec):** Out-of-the-box Gophish is easily fingerprinted. To improve stealth:
    *   **Header Modification:** Search the source code for `X-Gophish` headers and rename them (e.g., to `X-Contact`) using `sed` to avoid detection by email security gateways:
        ```bash
        find . -type f -exec sed -i.bak 's/X-Gophish-Contact/X-Contact/g' {} +
        ```
    *   **Infrastructure:** Use dedicated, reputable domains rather than default Gophish configurations. Always test against your own mail filters before full-scale deployment.

### Red Teaming: Command & Control (C2)
For internal red teaming, C2 frameworks facilitate post-exploitation and lateral movement testing.

*   **Sliver:** Currently favored for its versatility and cross-platform support (Windows, macOS, Linux). It supports multiple communication channels (mTLS, HTTPS, DNS), making it effective for testing egress filtering in complex network environments.
*   **Covenant:** A .NET-based framework ideal for environments heavily reliant on Windows/Active Directory.
    *   **Deployment:** Use Docker for rapid, isolated deployment.
    *   **Workflow:**
        1.  **Listener:** Configure a listener in the web UI (`https://localhost:7443`) to define how implants communicate back.
        2.  **Launcher:** Generate a payload (Grunt) tailored to the target OS.
        3.  **Execution:** Deploy the launcher on a test endpoint to establish a session.
*   **Operational Best Practice:** Always align exercises with the **MITRE ATT&CK** framework. In telecom environments, focus testing on lateral movement and privilege escalation within management planes (e.g., SSH, SNMP, or API-based infrastructure controls) rather than just endpoint compromise.

### Practical Implementation Checklist
1.  **Scope Definition:** Define clear "no-go" zones (e.g., core switching fabric, production billing databases) to prevent accidental outages.
2.  **Blue Team Coordination:** Use a "Purple Team" approach where defenders are aware of the simulation to maximize learning and validate detection logic.
3.  **Data Handling:** Ensure all captured credentials or sensitive data during simulations are handled according to internal data privacy policies and purged immediately post-exercise.

sections.title: Phishing Incident Triage and Investigation
sections.content:
### Phishing Incident Triage and Investigation

This section outlines the operational workflow for analyzing suspected phishing emails within a B2B telecom/networking environment.

#### 1. Initial Triage & Artifact Extraction
Upon receiving a report, immediately isolate the email artifact. Do not open attachments or click links. Use your mail gateway (e.g., Mimecast, Proofpoint, or O365 Defender) to export the message as an `.eml` or `.msg` file.

*   **Header Analysis:** Extract the `Authentication-Results` header to verify SPF, DKIM, and DMARC alignment.
    *   `spf=pass` / `dkim=pass` / `dmarc=pass` indicates the email originated from the claimed domain, suggesting a compromised account rather than spoofing.
*   **Command-Line Extraction:** Use `ripmime` or `exiftool` to safely extract attachments and metadata.
    ```bash
    # Extract attachments without executing
    ripmime -i suspicious_email.eml -d ./output_dir
    # Inspect metadata for malicious macros or hidden scripts
    exiftool -a -u -g1 suspicious_email.eml
    ```

#### 2. URL and Attachment Detonation
Never interact with suspicious URLs from a production machine.

*   **URL Analysis:** Use `curl` to inspect headers without downloading payloads.
    ```bash
    # Check for redirects or suspicious server headers
    curl -I -L -A "Mozilla/5.0" <SUSPICIOUS_URL>
    ```
*   **Reputation Checks:** Query VirusTotal or Cisco Talos via API to check for prior detections.
    ```bash
    # Example using VirusTotal API
    curl -X GET https://www.virustotal.com/api/v3/urls/<URL_ID> \
      -H "x-apikey: <YOUR_API_KEY>"
    ```
*   **Sandboxing:** Submit files to an isolated sandbox (e.g., Cuckoo, Joe Sandbox, or vendor-specific EDR sandbox) to observe behavioral indicators (C2 callbacks, registry modifications, process injection).

#### 3. Network-Level Investigation
In a telecom/networking environment, pivot from the email artifact to infrastructure logs.

*   **Log Correlation:** Search SIEM/Log Management (Splunk, ELK) for the identified IOCs (sender IP, malicious domain, file hash).
    *   **Query Example (Splunk):**
        `index=network_logs (src_ip=<SENDER_IP> OR dest_host=<MALICIOUS_DOMAIN>) | stats count by src_user, dest_host, action`
*   **DNS/Proxy Logs:** Check for outbound connections to the malicious domain. If internal hosts resolved the domain, identify the internal IP and initiate host-based containment.

#### 4. Containment and Remediation
If the investigation confirms a phishing attempt:

1.  **Global Purge:** Use PowerShell (Exchange Online) or API-based tools to remove the email from all user mailboxes.
    ```powershell
    # Exchange Online purge example
    Search-Mailbox -Identity "user@example.com" -SearchQuery 'Subject:"Urgent Invoice"' -DeleteContent
    ```
2.  **Block IOCs:**
    *   **Firewall/Proxy:** Block the malicious domain/IP at the edge.
    *   **Gateway:** Add the sender domain or specific file hash to the global blocklist.
3.  **Credential Reset:** If logs indicate a user clicked a link and navigated to a credential harvesting site, force a password reset and revoke active O365/SSO sessions immediately.
4.  **Endpoint Scan:** Trigger an EDR scan (CrowdStrike, SentinelOne) on the affected host to search for dropped payloads or persistence mechanisms.

glossary.definition: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability — the three properties security controls aim to protect.
Security model that never trusts a request based on network location alone; every request is authenticated and authorized.
Multi-Factor Authentication — requiring two or more distinct proof-of-identity categories.
Time-based One-Time Password (RFC 6238) — the algorithm behind authenticator apps.
Phishing-resistant authentication standard using hardware or platform keys bound to the origin domain.
Public Key Infrastructure — the system of CAs, certificates, and keys that establishes trust for TLS and signing.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — a public identifier for a specific known vulnerability.
Common Vulnerability Scoring System — a 0-10 severity score for a vulnerability.
Endpoint Detection and Response — behavioral endpoint security with remote investigation/response capability.
Security Information and Event Management — centralized log collection, correlation, and alerting.
Indicator of Compromise — an artifact (hash, IP, domain) suggesting a system has been breached.
A vulnerability being exploited before a patch is available.
Granting only the minimum access needed to perform a function.
Layering multiple independent security controls so no single failure causes full compromise.
An attacker's technique of moving from an initial compromised host to other systems within a network.

commonIssues.problem: User approves an unexpected MFA push notification
commonIssues.cause: Attacker has valid stolen credentials and spams push requests until the user taps accept out of habit or annoyance (MFA fatigue)
commonIssues.solution: Switch to number-matching push or FIDO2 hardware keys; investigate and force password reset + session revocation immediately after any accidental approval

commonIssues.problem: Same password reused across multiple services gets compromised
commonIssues.cause: Password reuse means a breach at any one service exposes accounts elsewhere (credential stuffing)
commonIssues.solution: Enforce unique passwords via a password manager, check new passwords against breached-password lists, and require MFA everywhere so a leaked password alone isn't enough

commonIssues.problem: Public-facing service exploited via a CVE that had a patch available for months
commonIssues.cause: Patch management gap — patch existed but wasn't prioritized or deployed
commonIssues.solution: Cross-reference vulnerabilities against CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and patch those first regardless of CVSS score; track compliance, not just patch release

commonIssues.problem: Employee clicks a phishing link and enters credentials on a fake login page
commonIssues.cause: Convincing spoofed page, lack of FIDO2/phishing-resistant MFA, insufficient email filtering (SPF/DKIM/DMARC gaps)
commonIssues.solution: Force password reset + revoke sessions immediately, review for lateral movement, and move toward FIDO2/WebAuthn which is cryptographically bound to the real origin

commonIssues.problem: Exposed RDP port gets brute-forced and used as initial access for ransomware
commonIssues.cause: RDP directly reachable from the internet with only a password for protection
commonIssues.solution: Never expose RDP directly — require VPN or a jump host with MFA in front of it, and enable account lockout/rate limiting as defense in depth

commonIssues.problem: Cloud storage bucket found publicly readable, exposing customer data
commonIssues.cause: Misconfigured access policy — default-open bucket or overly broad IAM permission
commonIssues.solution: Audit storage ACLs regularly with cloud security posture tools, default to private, and require an explicit, reviewed change to make anything public

commonIssues.problem: Ransomware encrypts file shares across multiple servers within minutes
commonIssues.cause: Attacker obtained domain admin or a highly-privileged service account and moved laterally via SMB admin shares before detonating
commonIssues.solution: Segment networks, restrict admin share access, monitor for unusual SMB/authentication activity, and maintain offline/immutable backups untouched by the compromised domain

commonIssues.problem: Security incident investigation has no useful logs to reconstruct what happened
commonIssues.cause: Logging disabled or retained too briefly, or logs stored only on the compromised host itself
commonIssues.solution: Ship logs centrally (SIEM/syslog) with retention long enough to cover realistic dwell time, and treat 'logging enabled and shipped off-host' as a baseline control, not optional

commonIssues.problem: Former employee's account still has active access weeks after departure
commonIssues.cause: No automated offboarding tied to HR system; manual deprovisioning was missed
commonIssues.solution: Tie account deactivation to HR offboarding workflows automatically, and periodically audit active accounts against current employee/contractor lists

commonIssues.problem: TLS certificate expires unexpectedly and breaks a production service
commonIssues.cause: No automated renewal/monitoring for certificate expiry
commonIssues.solution: Use automated renewal (ACME/Let's Encrypt or an internal PKI with auto-renewal) and monitor expiry dates with alerting well before the deadline
